@engine/ai 0.1.0

Navigation grid built from the level, A* paths (resumable), steering, behaviour trees and perception; the arena's bots are built from it.

51 of 51 exports have a description. npm install @engine/ai

class class NavGrid

A grid of the walkable floor in a level, built once from its collision triangles: a height per cell, several floors per column (stairs, bridges), cells too close to walls removed for the agent's radius, and links for drops and small gaps. Create it with NavGrid.build(world, options) and search it with findPath.

constructor(o)

Use NavGrid.build(world, options).

static build(world, options)
NameTypeDescription
worldimport('../../physics/src/tri-world.js').TriWorldA built world. Triangles should be wound so their normal points out of the solid (boxes and glTF meshes are); a floor below another surface counts only if it faces up.
optionsNavOptions
get walkableCount

Number of nodes an agent can stand on.

columnAt(x, z)

The cell column holding a world position, or -1 outside the grid.

nearest(x, y, z, maxCells = 6)

The walkable node nearest a point: the best floor in its column (preferring one at about the same height), else the nearest cell in rings around it, up to maxCells away.

Returns number — node index, or -1

setArea(minX, minY, minZ, maxX, maxY, maxZ, kind)

Set the kind of ground inside a box (e.g. water, mud) and give each kind a cost multiplier with areaCost[kind] = 3.

block(minX, minY, minZ, maxX, maxY, maxZ, margin = this.agentRadius)

Keep agents out of a box (a closed door, a barricade, a spreading fire). Nodes within margin of it become impassable until unblock. Returns a handle.

unblock(id)
addLink(from, to, { cost = null, bidirectional = true } = {})

Connect two nodes by something that is not walking: a jump, a ladder, a teleporter. cost is in metres of walking it is worth.

lineOfWalk(a, b, costLimit = Infinity)

Can an agent walk in a straight line between two nodes along the grid (every step of the line is a real connection)? Used to smooth paths and to test "can I just go there". costLimit: refuse to walk through ground costlier than this (a swamp).

static build(vertices, indices, options = {})

Make a navigation mesh from triangles (the level's collision triangles will do: it keeps the ones an agent can stand on).

NameTypeDescription
verticesArrayLike<number>x, y, z for each vertex
indicesArrayLike<number>three vertex numbers for each triangle
options optionalNavMeshOptions
constructor(vertices, indices, { maxSlope = 45, maxEdge = Infinity, agentRadius = 0.4, weld = 0.0001 } = {})
edge(p, e)

The corners of a triangle's edge e (the edge from corner e to corner e + 1, both vertex numbers).

contains(p, x, z)

Whether (x, z) is over triangle p.

heightAt(p, x, z)

The height of triangle p at (x, z).

polyAt(x, y, z, maxDy = Infinity)

The triangle under a point: the one whose surface at (x, z) is nearest to height y, within maxDy (so a bridge and the ground under it are told apart). -1 if there is none.

NameTypeDescription
maxDy optionalnumber
nearest(x, y, z, radius = 2, blocked = false)

The nearest place on the mesh to a point (not counting blocked triangles unless blocked), looking up to radius away.

Returns {poly: number, x: number, y: number, z: number, distance: number} | null

randomPoint(random)

A point on the mesh chosen with random() (a function giving numbers from 0 up to 1; pass your game's seeded generator) from a triangle that is not blocked, or null.

block(minX, minY, minZ, maxX, maxY, maxZ, margin = 0)

Block everything inside a box (a crate, a barricade, a closed door) so paths go round. Triangles the box touches cannot be entered, so cut big triangles smaller with maxEdge when you build the mesh to keep the blocked patch close to the shape. Returns a number for unblock.

NameTypeDescription
marginnumberMake the box this much bigger on every side
blockCircle(x, z, radius, minY = -Infinity, maxY = Infinity)

Block a circle on the ground (a pillar, a stopped vehicle) between two heights. Returns a number for unblock.

unblock(id)

Take an obstacle away.

setArea(minX, minY, minZ, maxX, maxY, maxZ, kind)

Mark the ground inside a box as a kind (0 normal; give a kind a cost with areaCost[kind] = 3 for mud, water, a road to keep to).

findPath(from, to, { radius = this.agentRadius, partial = false, snap = 2, maxNodes = 100000, smooth = true } = {})

The shortest walk from one place to another, held off the corners of walls by the agent's radius.

NameTypeDescription
from{x: number, y: number, z: number}
to{x: number, y: number, z: number}
o optionalobject
o.radius optionalnumberDistance to keep from corners (default: the mesh's agentRadius).
o.partial optionalbooleanWhen the goal cannot be reached, go as near as possible instead of failing.
o.snap optionalnumberHow far from the mesh the start and goal may be and still count (2 metres).
o.maxNodes optionalnumberGive up after looking at this many triangles (100000).
o.smooth optionalbooleanCut out corners that a straight walk the width of the agent can skip (default true): the corridor search is close to the shortest route but not exact.

Returns NavPath

canWalk(x, y, z, tx, tz, radius = this.agentRadius)

Whether an agent radius wide standing at (x, y, z) can walk straight to (tx, tz) without a wall in the way (see isVisible for a point-sized one).

move(poly, x, z, tx, tz)

Move along the surface from a place in triangle poly toward (tx, tz): the walk passes from triangle to triangle and slides along a wall it meets instead of passing through.

Returns {poly: number, x: number, y: number, z: number, hit: boolean} — where it ended up; hit says a wall stopped it

raycast(from, to)

Walk a straight line over the mesh from a point to another and report where a wall stops it, if one does.

Returns {hit: boolean, t: number, x: number, y: number, z: number, poly: number} — t is how far along the line (0 to 1) it got

isVisible(from, to)

Whether a straight walk between two points is free of walls (the path can be shortened to it).

findPath(from, to, o = {})

Find a path. The start and the goal are moved to the nearest free place if they are inside something. weight above 1 trades a little length for a lot of speed (the search leans toward the goal: a path at most weight times the best, found by looking at far fewer cubes).

NameTypeDescription
fromnumber[]
tonumber[]
o optional{maxNodes?: number, smooth?: boolean, weight?: number}

Returns {status: 'found' | 'partial' | 'none', path: number[][], cost: number} — partial means the goal cannot be reached; the path ends as near to it as the search got.

request(from, to, o = {})

Ask for a path to be found a little at a time: the answer comes when pump has spent enough effort on it, so a long search never holds up a frame. Searches are done one after another, in the order they were asked for. Watch done (then read result) on what it returns; cancel() drops a request that is no longer wanted.

NameTypeDescription
fromnumber[]
tonumber[]
o optional{maxNodes?: number, smooth?: boolean, weight?: number}

Returns {done: boolean, result: {status: 'found' | 'partial' | 'none', path: number[][], cost: number} | null, cancel: () => void}

pump(budget, tick = undefined)

Spend up to budget cubes of searching on the requests that are waiting. Call it once a tick (a second call in the same tick does nothing, so every caller may call it).

NameTypeDescription
budgetnumber
tick optionalnumbera number that changes every tick

Returns number — how many cubes were looked at

smoothPath(points)

Pull the path straight: from each point, jump to the furthest later point that can be reached in a straight line. Internal: used by PathSearch.

NameTypeDescription
maxSlope optionalnumberSteepest slope walked, in degrees (45); steeper triangles, and ceilings, are not part of the mesh.

class class Lockstep

The agreement between two (or more) computers about whose keys count on which tick. Each tick: call local(keys) once with the keys this player holds *now* (it gives back the message to send); call receive(message) for every message from the others; and simulate a tick only if ready(), taking take() for the keys of every player. The keys held on tick t are used on tick t + delay, so the first delay ticks run with nobody holding anything. Messages may arrive late, twice, or out of order; they never need to arrive in any particular order.

constructor({ players = 2, me = 0, delay = 3, window = 240, checkEvery = 60 } = {})
NameTypeDescription
o optionalobject
o.players optionalnumberHow many players (default 2).
o.me optionalnumberThis player's number (0 is the host).
o.delay optionalnumberTicks between pressing a key and the game using it (default 3: a twentieth of a second).
o.window optionalnumberThe most ticks a friend's keys may be ahead of this computer before they are refused (default 240).
o.checkEvery optionalnumberEvery this many ticks the computers compare a fingerprint of the game, to notice at once if they ever disagree (default 60).
local(keys)

Choose this player's keys for a tick delay ticks from now, once per tick.

NameTypeDescription
keysIterable<string>The keys held now.

Returns {t: 'in', f: number, k: string[]} | null — The message to send to the others, or null if this tick's keys were already chosen.

receive(message, from)

Take in a message from another computer.

NameTypeDescription
messageunknown
fromnumberWhich player sent it.

Returns boolean — False if it was refused.

ready()

Has every player's keys for the next tick arrived?

take()

The keys of every player for the tick about to be simulated: one Set per player. Call only when ready(); then simulate the tick, and call done.

Returns Set<string>[]

done(hash)

The tick has been simulated. Pass a fingerprint of the game now (only needed on the ticks wantsSum says; otherwise leave it out).

NameTypeDescription
hash optionalstring

Returns {t: 'sum', f: number, h: string} | null — A message to send, when this is a tick to compare on.

wantsSum(frame)

Is the game after frame ticks one the computers compare?

NameTypeDescription
framenumber

IMA ADPCM: four bits a sample, about 8 KB/s at 16 kHz mono, a quarter of 16-bit PCM and cheap enough to run in plain JavaScript anywhere. Each frame starts with the encoder's state, so a lost frame never damages the next one. Speech comes through clearly; it is not as small as Opus.

class class AudioEngine

Sound for games on the Web Audio API: a mixer of named buses (master, sfx, music, ui, voice, or your own), voice limiting with priorities, positional sound relative to a listener (distance fall-off and left/right panning), music with cross-fades, and sounds that can be made in code (see synth.js) so a game needs no audio files to start. Browsers keep audio silent until the player has interacted with the page; the engine listens for the first click, key press or touch and starts then (unlockOnGesture). Until it is running, one-shot sounds are skipped (a burst of stale sounds would play the moment it unlocks) while looping music is kept waiting.

class class JitterBuffer

Packets cross a network late, out of order, twice or not at all; speech has to come out at an even pace. The jitter buffer holds a few frames back (the *delay*), puts them in order, and on each tick of the playback clock (pull, once per frame) gives the next frame, or says one is missing so the player can cover the gap. The delay adapts: it grows when packets keep arriving too late to use and shrinks again when the network is steady. A burst of speech ends with an end packet, after which the buffer goes quiet until the next burst.

constructor({ targetFrames = 3, minFrames = 2, maxFrames = 15, maxBuffered = 30, maxConceal = 8, adaptive = true } = {})

o.maxBuffered optionalnumberFrames held before the oldest are dropped to catch up (30).

src/voices.js:20

class class VoiceRouter

The server's side of voice chat: given who is talking and who is listening, decides who hears them and how loudly. Pure logic (no sockets): your game sends the packet to each returned id. Modes: 'proximity' (within maxDistance, fading with distance), 'team' (same team, any distance), 'global' (everyone). A speaker can also be on a private channel (a party), heard only by listeners on the same one.

class class VoiceSender

Turns frames from a microphone into packets: decides whether to send (voice activity, push-to-talk or muted), encodes, numbers the packets, and marks the end of each burst of speech. function function dopplerRatio(listener, listenerVelocity, position, velocity, speedOfSound = 343, strength = 1)

Doppler shift: how much higher (above 1) or lower (below 1) a moving source sounds to a moving listener. A source coming at you, or you going at it, raises the pitch; going away lowers it. Only the speeds along the line between the two count. The result is held to 0.5..2 so a shout across a supersonic gap cannot make noise.

class class InterpolationClock

Decides which server tick to draw other entities at.

Snapshots arrive "late" by the network latency plus some queueing jitter. For smooth interpolation we render slightly in the past: far enough behind the newest snapshot that the next one has (almost always) arrived, but no further, because every extra tick of delay is visible lag.

Measured per snapshot: - lateness m: smoothed (arrival time in ticks - snapshot tick), i.e. the latency floor plus average queueing; - jitter d: smoothed mean deviation of lateness (RFC 3550 style); - gap: spacing between accepted snapshot ticks (1 normally, larger when packets are lost). The buffer follows a slowly decaying *peak* of the gap, not its mean, because one lost snapshot must not starve rendering; - step detection: if lateness stays far from its estimate for several snapshots (a route change), the estimate jumps to the new level at once instead of crawling there.

Buffer depth = peak gap + k * jitter, clamped. The defaults (k = 4, minimum 2 ticks) came from sweeping the arena network lab (tools/arena-netlab-sweep.js): with k = 3 and a 1.5 tick minimum, a link with only 10 ms of jitter starved 4% of frames; k = 4 with a 2 tick minimum removed that at a cost of ~8 ms. The render clock then slews toward now - m - buffer by speeding up or slowing down at most maxRateAdjust, so a changing target never makes motion visibly jump, and it only snaps when the target moves far away (e.g. a route change).

constructor({ tickMs, k = 4, minBufferTicks = 2, maxBufferTicks = 20, maxRateAdjust = 0.1, gain = 0.2, snapTicks = 8, stepTicks = 6, fixedDelayMs = null })

Types

type FlatState

A flat object of numbers.

type RollbackOptions

NameTypeDescription
playersnumberHow many players.
localnumberWhich player is on this machine (0 to players - 1).
init() => anyMakes the state at frame 0.
step(state: any, inputs: any[], frame: number) => voidSimulates one frame, changing the state in place. inputs[p] is player p's input for this frame.
clone optional(state: any) => anyCopies a state. Default structuredClone (so the state must be plain data).
maxRollback optionalnumberThe most frames it may run ahead of what is confirmed (and so the most it ever re-simulates). Default 8.
inputDelay optionalnumberLocal inputs take effect this many frames late, which gives the other player time to receive them and so means fewer rollbacks. Default 0.
blank optionalanyThe input that means "nothing pressed", used for the first frames and before anything is known. Default null.
assumeBlank optionalbooleanTreat the first inputDelay frames as known (blank) for every player. Default true; pass false when a server decides every input, including those of the first frames.
serverDecides optionalbooleanA server has the last word on every input, this machine's own included: a command may be given again for a frame it was already given for (the newest is the one to send), so the lead of the local inputs over the present frame follows inputDelay both ways (but is never for a frame the server has already decided: setInput for this machine's own seat moves that line). Default false (peers: each frame's input is given once, so a lead that grew can never shrink).
guess optional(last: any) => anyGuesses an input that has not arrived from the last one that did. Default: the same again.
checksum optional(state: any) => numberA number that says what a state is, to find players that disagree.
startFrame optionalnumberThe frame init gives the state of (default 0): a player who joins a game that is already going starts from the state they were sent, at the frame it was.

function function snapAngle(axis, start, angle, targets, { threshold })

Snap the angle of a turn about an axis so that the turned thing's sides run parallel to the sides of something else (the world's axes, another object, the 3D cursor). For each side of the thing and each side of a target it works out the angle that makes them parallel (in the plane the turn happens in; a side that points along the axis does not turn and is left out), and takes the one nearest the angle asked for if it is within reach. Sides count in both directions, so a box also meets a target a quarter turn away.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
axisnumber[]the unit axis of the turn (world)
startnumber[]the thing's orientation before the turn, a quaternion [x, y, z, w]
anglenumberthe turn asked for, radians
targetsnumber[][]orientations to line up with (quaternions)
o{threshold: number}how close (radians) before it jumps

Returns {angle: number, target: number, from: number[], to: number[]} | null — the snapped angle, which target it met (an index into targets), and the directions of the thing's side and the target's side (after the turn) that are now parallel; null when nothing is in reach

class class AnimationGraph

Blends animation clips driven by parameters and triggers: states that play a clip or a 1D blend tree, transitions on parameter conditions, triggers or finished clips, cross-fades and interrupts. update(dt) advances it and sample(...) gives the pose to draw.

io.skeleton{createPose: () => any}Whatever makes a pose you can pass to sample and blend.
io.sample(skeleton: any, clip: any, time: number, out: any) => voidWrite the pose of clip at time seconds into out.
io.blend(out: any, a: any, b: any, weight: number) => voidout = a * (1 - weight) + b * weight.

class class StateMachine

A hierarchical state machine: states with enter / update / exit, transitions on events, conditions and timers with priorities, "from any" transitions, nested machines inside states (with history), loop detection and save / load. Can be defined from plain data.

constructor(config, { name = 'machine' } = {})
NameTypeDescription
config{initial: string, states: Record<string, StateConfig>, any?: Transition[]}
o optional{name?: string}
get path

The active state path: "combat/aiming".

is(path)

Is the machine in this state (a name, or a path prefix like "combat" while in "combat/aiming")?

start(ctx)

Enter the initial state. Called for you by the first update or send.

go(ctx, to, { action, history = false, event = null } = {})

Move to another state now. to is relative to this machine: a sibling ("run"), a state inside a sibling ("combat/aiming"), or up through the machines around it ("../dead" from inside "combat").

NameTypeDescription
o optional{action?: Function, history?: boolean, event?: string | null}
update(dt, ctx)

Advance time, follow transitions that are due, and run the current states' updates (parents first).

send(event, ctx)

Tell the machine something happened. The deepest state that has a transition for it handles it.

Returns boolean — whether a transition was taken

post(event)

Remember an event to be handled at the end of the next update (for code that runs mid-frame).

save()

Where the machine is, as plain data (state path, time in each level, remembered history, memory).

load(data)

Put the machine back where save() found it. Enter / exit functions are not called (the world is restored separately).

function function screenDirection(eye, target, yaw, pitch)

Which way, on the screen, a place is from the crosshair: the angle of the arrow that points to it (0 is to the right, a quarter turn is down), and how far in front of the view it is (1 straight ahead, -1 straight behind). It is worked out in the camera's own directions (right, up, forward), so it is true whatever the camera's pitch: looking up at the sky, a place below and in front points down, and one behind you points up (the shortest way to face it is over the top), each to the side it really is on. The camera's convention is the one of this engine's renderer: yaw 0 looks along -z, and a positive pitch looks up.

class class GestureRecognizer

Gestures from raw pointers: tap, double tap, long press, swipe, one- and two-finger pan, pinch and rotate. It works on plain numbers (an id, a position, a time in milliseconds), so a touch screen, a pen, a mouse, a test and a replay all feed it the same way; attachGestures connects a page.

One pointer: a short press without moving is a tap (a second one close in time and place is a tap with count: 2); held still it becomes a longpress; dragged it is a pan, and a quick, long enough flick that ends the pan is also a swipe. Two pointers: a pan of their centre, a pinch (the scale of the distance between them) and a rotate (the turn of the line between them). Putting a second finger down cancels a tap in progress.

Gesture objects: {type, x, y, ...} where x and y are where it happened (the centre, for two fingers). pan, pinch and rotate carry a phase of 'start', 'move' or 'end'.

constructor({ tapMs = 250, tapSlop = 10, doubleTapMs = 300, doubleTapSlop = 30, longPressMs = 500, swipeMinDistance = 40, swipeMaxMs = 500, swipeMinSpeed = 250, pinchSlop = 8, rotateSlop = 0.12, onGesture = null } = {})
NameTypeDescription
o optionalobject

o.doubleTapMs optionalnumberLongest gap between the two taps of a double tap (300).
o.doubleTapSlop optionalnumberHow far apart they may be (30).
o.longPressMs optionalnumberHow long a finger held still becomes a long press (500).
o.swipeMinDistance optionalnumberA flick shorter than this (pixels) is not a swipe (40).
o.swipeMaxMs optionalnumberA flick slower than this in total is not a swipe (500).

o.rotateSlop optionalnumberHow far the line between them must turn (radians) before a rotation starts (0.12).

src/gestures.js:12

class class InputCore

Device-independent input. You describe what the player can DO (actions: jump, fire, move, look) and what controls do it (bindings: a key, a button, a stick, an on-screen control); the game reads actions once per frame. The core knows nothing about the browser: adapters (see devices.js) feed it raw events, and tests can feed it directly. Reading: call update(dt) once per frame, then held('fire'), pressed('jump'), released(...), value('zoom'), vector('move'). Vectors from a pointing device or a stick-as-look are per-frame turns in radians (right and up are +); vectors from keys or sticks are unit vectors (length at most 1).

type Gesture

Gestures from raw pointers: tap, double tap, long press, swipe, one- and two-finger pan, pinch and rotate. It works on plain numbers (an id, a position, a time in milliseconds), so a touch screen, a pen, a mouse, a test and a replay all feed it the same way; attachGestures connects a page.

One pointer: a short press without moving is a tap (a second one close in time and place is a tap with count: 2); held still it becomes a longpress; dragged it is a pan, and a quick, long enough flick that ends the pan is also a swipe. Two pointers: a pan of their centre, a pinch (the scale of the distance between them) and a rotate (the turn of the line between them). Putting a second finger down cancels a tap in progress.

Gesture objects: {type, x, y, ...} where x and y are where it happened (the centre, for two fingers). pan, pinch and rotate carry a phase of 'start', 'move' or 'end'.

type Stroke

type StrokeSample

A stroke as a pen (or finger, or mouse) draws it: a list of samples with position, pressure, tilt and time. StrokeRecorder turns a stream of pointer positions into strokes (thinning out samples that barely moved, smoothing jitter, keeping the high-rate samples a pen reports between frames), and penWidth turns pressure into a brush width. The pieces take plain numbers, so a test or a replay can draw too; attachPenStrokes connects a page.

type TouchControl

class class Matchmaker

The matchmaking queue. Players (alone or in parties) enqueue for a mode; tick() turns the queue into matches: similar ratings and even teams first, looser rules the longer someone has waited, a partly filled match after relaxAfterMs, and tickets that waited too long come back as expired. No timers, network or randomness inside: you pass the clock and call tick().

node class class MatchService

The matchmaking service: a Matchmaker, a timer that ticks it, and an HTTP handler.

POST /queue { mode, players?: [ids], region?, meta? } -> 201 { ticket } GET /ticket/<id> -> { status: 'waiting' | 'matched' | 'expired' | 'cancelled', ... } (matched: { room, token, team, match }) DELETE /ticket/<id> -> 204 GET /status -> { modes: { duel: { tickets, players, estimatedWaitMs } } }

userOf(req) says who is calling (your login check); a caller may only queue as themselves, and as a party only players canParty allows.

namespace namespace mat4

4x4 matrices as plain arrays or Float32Array/Float64Array of 16, COLUMN-major (element [column * 4 + row]), the layout both WebGPU and WebGL expect, so a matrix can be uploaded as it is. Output-first and allocation-free, like vec3 and quat. Right-handed, +y up, the camera looks down -z. perspective and orthographic give clip-space depth in [0, 1] (WebGPU's convention; the WebGL2 renderer remaps it in the vertex shader). Deterministic: only + - * / and sqrt, plus this package's own sin, cos and tan.

A model matrix from a position, a rotation quaternion and a scale (the usual translate * rotate * scale).

node class class ModManager

Loads mods, runs script mods in confined sandboxes, and turns what they return into validated commands.

The game integrates in four steps: add bundles, start(), emitFrame(frame) on a timer (non-blocking), and drainCommands() each tick to apply what mods asked for. Slow or misbehaving mods are skipped, struck, and eventually disabled; none of this can block the caller.

node class class ModSandbox

One mod, in its own confined process. Started with: --permission (no filesystem except reading the engine's own sandbox files, no child processes, no workers), --max-old-space-size (a runaway allocation kills the child, not the server), --disallow-code-generation-from-strings (even the child's own realm cannot eval), a scrubbed environment, no stdio, and below-normal OS priority. It does NOT block the network (Node 24's permission model does not cover it): see SECURITY.md.

Types

type Bundle

A bundle is a manifest plus its files as text, plus an optional signature. The hash covers the manifest and all files, so it identifies exactly what will run. The *client view* is the data clients need (rules and client); it has its own hash, which the server advertises and clients verify before playing.

NameTypeDescription
manifestimport('./manifest.js').ModManifest
filesRecord<string, string>path -> text (the entry script, extra data files)
signature optional{key: string, sig: string} | nullEd25519: raw public key (hex) and signature over the bundle hash (hex).

type CommandSpecs

op name -> field name -> spec

type FieldSpec

Mods act on the game only through *commands*: small JSON objects the game defines and validates. The mod proposes, the game decides (and can refuse). A command spec lists exactly the allowed fields and their types.

type ModManifest

A mod's mod.json. Strict on purpose: unknown fields are errors, so typos do not silently do nothing and a manifest cannot smuggle in fields a future version might interpret.

node class class FileStore

Records as JSON files in a folder: <dir>/<namespace>/<two hex digits>/<key>.json, each written to a temporary file and renamed into place, so a crash never leaves half a record. Writes to one record are queued, so version checks are exact inside one server process. Use it for one server (or one server per folder); several servers sharing records need a database behind the same Store contract. list reads folder names: fine for thousands of records, not for millions.

class class CharacterController

A first- or third-person character body: walks on slopes, climbs steps, falls, jumps, stands still without jitter and slides down surfaces that are too steep. Collision is an ellipsoid swept through a TriWorld, so nothing tunnels at any speed. One update is one tick: the same function runs on the server (authoritative) and in the client (prediction), and uses only + - * / and sqrt, so both get the same bits on every engine.

Coordinates: +y up. x, y, z is the centre of the body; the feet are at y - halfHeight.

class class PoseInterpolator

Blends each body between where it was before the last physics step and where it is now, so drawing at any frame rate looks smooth. Works with World2D (bodies with x, y, c, s) and PhysicsWorld (bodies with x, y, z and a quaternion); rotations are blended the short way round.

``js const view = new PoseInterpolator(world); // in the fixed update: view.snapshot(); world.step(dt); // in the render, with the loop's alpha: const p = view.pose(body, alpha, pose); draw at p.x, p.y, p.angle ``

class class RaycastVehicle

A car, bike, cart, hovercraft or anything else that rolls on springs. The chassis is an ordinary dynamic RigidBody in the world; each wheel casts a ray down from its fixing, pushes the chassis up with a spring and damper where it hits, and grips the ground sideways and along (engine, brakes, rolling resistance) up to what its load allows (a friction circle: a wheel that is braking hard has less grip to turn with). Call update(dt) once per tick, before world.step(dt). Chassis axes: forward (default +z) and up (default +y) in its own coordinates; positive steering turns toward the right, the side your right hand is on looking along forward with up overhead (with forward +z that is -x).

class class TriWorld

Static 3D collision geometry: a triangle soup indexed by a uniform 3D grid (typed arrays, built once). Everything the 3D character controller, hitscan and line-of-sight need: queryAabb (candidates for a moving shape) and raycast. Boxes, quads and arbitrary indexed meshes (a glTF's positions and indices) all become triangles. Conventions: right-handed, +y up (see @engine/math). Triangles are two-sided, so winding only matters for normal* (outward by the right-hand rule: (b - a) x (c - a)). Usage: add geometry, call build() once, then query. Adding after build() requires another build().

function function moveEllipsoid(world, px, py, pz, vx, vy, vz, rx, ry, rz, out, wallBelowY = 0, stopAtContact = false)

Move an ellipsoid (a character body) through static triangle geometry and slide along what it hits. The motion is a continuous sweep, so no speed can carry it through a surface (even a single zero-thickness triangle), and the result is the same bits on every engine. Works in "ellipsoid space": every coordinate divided by the radii makes the body a unit sphere, which is what the narrow phase sweeps.

Up to 5 contacts are processed; when the motion is jammed between two surfaces it slides along their crease, and between three it stops.

class class SnapshotHistory

Fixed ring of recent snapshots, looked up by tick. The server keeps one per client (or one shared) to find the acked baseline for deltas; the client keeps one to decode incoming deltas.

Usage: slot = h.acquire(), fill it (capture/decode), then h.commit(slot). A slot that was acquired but never committed (e.g. decode threw) is never returned by get, so a half-written snapshot can't become a baseline. Acquiring evicts the oldest entry, so size the ring larger than the longest ack lag you want to serve deltas for; beyond that, get returns undefined and the sender falls back to a full snapshot.

class class DrawList3D

The meshes to draw this frame, grouped by mesh so each one becomes a single instanced draw call. Reuse one list every frame: clear(), then add... for everything visible. Lighting uses the model matrix's rotation for normals, so non-uniform scaling skews the shading a little; scale uniformly where it matters.

constructor()
setMaterial(layer, mapping = 'uv', scale = 1)

Texture the instances you add next (until the next call, or clear()). The layer is what TextureSet.add returned. - 'uv': use the mesh's texture coordinates (meshes without any show one texel), multiplied by scale (2 = the texture repeats twice). - 'planar': no coordinates needed: the texture is projected along whichever world axis the surface faces most, scale times per metre (0.25 = one repeat per 4 m). Good for ground, walls and boxes; the texture stays put as objects move around it. The instance colour multiplies the texture, so a white texture shows the colour and a coloured one tints it.

NameTypeDescription
layernumber | null
mapping optional'uv' | 'planar'
scale optionalnumber
setBlended(on = true)

Draw the instances you add next as translucent: after everything solid, blended over it by their alpha, and writing no depth, so what is behind a pane of glass, a force field or a bubble shows through it (and so do the particles, which are drawn after the solid things too: without this, a see-through instance hides them, because it has written the depth in front of them). They cast no shadow. Instances of the same mesh are drawn in the order they were added; give the far one first when two overlap and the order shows. Skinned instances are not affected. clear() turns it off.

NameTypeDescription
on optionalboolean
setSurface(id = 0)

Draw the instances you add next (until the next call, or clear()) with a physically based material from the MaterialSet the renderer was given (renderer.setMaterials): a number MaterialSet.add returned. Such a surface is lit with metal and roughness, bump and occlusion pictures and emission instead of the simple lighting, and takes its pictures from the material, so setMaterial has no effect on it; the instance colour still tints it. Pass 0 (or nothing) to go back to the simple lighting.

id optionalnumber
setWater(style = 0, time = 0)

Draw the instances you add next as water (see createWaterMesh and createWaterStyle): lifted by waves, coloured by depth, reflecting the sky. style is an index into lighting.water (0 to 3), time the clock in seconds that moves the waves. Add water after the solid things, with an alpha below 0.5 so it casts no shadow. Anything set with setMaterial, setSurface or setTerrain afterwards replaces this.

Texture the instances you add next as terrain: ground that blends four pictures by a splat map. splatLayer is a layer of the TextureSet whose red, green, blue and alpha say how much of the first, second, third and fourth picture shows at each place (stretched over the terrain by the mesh's texture coordinates, so give the terrain mesh uv running 0 to 1 over the whole terrain); firstLayer is the first of four layers in a row that hold the pictures. class class Font

Text as ordinary sprites. Each glyph is drawn once, in white, into the shared atlas by the browser's own text engine (any installed or web font, emoji, accents, CJK), then drawn like any other sprite and coloured by the tint. So text costs no extra draw call, works identically in all three backends, and sorts with everything else. Glyphs are rasterised at size * scale pixels and drawn at size world units, so for crisp text pass scale: devicePixelRatio and draw it with a screen-space camera (Camera.setScreenSpace), where one world unit is one CSS pixel. Text in a zoomed world camera gets blurry or blocky; make a Font at the size you need. Pass sdf: true (or { size, spread }) for scalable text: glyphs are stored as signed distance fields and the shader draws a sharp anti-aliased edge at any size, rotation or camera zoom (stored once at about 48 px, drawn from 8 to several hundred world units). It costs a one-off distance transform per glyph and is a little softer than hinted raster text at small sizes (under about 14 px), so use plain Font for small UI text and sdf for the rest. Plain Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and CJK text is laid out glyph by glyph (per-glyph advances, no kerning), with \n line breaks and optional word wrap. Text that needs more goes through the layout engine (see textlayout.js) without your doing anything: right-to-left and mixed-direction text is reordered (bidi.js), words in Arabic, Hebrew, Indic and Southeast Asian scripts are shaped by the browser as whole words, and an emoji with its skin tone or a letter with accents is one unit.

constant const INSTANCE_WORDS

Every backend draws the same instance buffer: one quad per sprite, 11 words (44 bytes) each, so switching renderer changes only upload and draw calls. word 0-1 x, y centre in world units word 2-3 w, h size in world units (a negative w draws the sprite mirrored left to right) word 4 rotation radians word 5-8 u0 v0 u1 v1 atlas rectangle, normalised 0..1 word 9 tint RGBA8, little-endian (R in the lowest byte); see packTint word 10 meta atlas page in bits 0-7, flags above: bit 8 = signed-distance-field sprite (text), bit 9 = ignores 2D lighting Draw order is push order unless sprites are given a sort key (see push and sort). The key is NOT part of the instance data: it lives in a parallel array and never reaches the GPU.

Value: 11

src/meshbatch.js:17

constant const MESH_VERTEX_WORDS

Flat triangles for the 2D renderers: whatever a quad cannot do (a deforming skeleton mesh, a rope, a flag, a torn sprite). Every vertex has a position in world units, a place in the atlas, a tint and an atlas page, so one MeshBatch2D is one draw call whatever it holds. Draw it with renderer.render({ camera, batch, meshes }): meshes are drawn after the sprites of the same call (use renderLayers to interleave). Each vertex is 6 words (24 bytes): word 0-1 x, y position in world units word 2-3 u, v position in the atlas page, 0..1 (use the sprite's u0 v0 u1 v1 range) word 4 tint RGBA8, see packTint (straight alpha; the shader premultiplies) word 5 meta atlas page in bits 0-7; bit 10 = additive (the colour is added to what is behind it instead of covering it)

Value: 6

class class MorphTargets

Morph targets (blend shapes): a mesh that can change shape by mixing in stored offsets, such as a face that smiles, blinks and talks. Each target is a set of offsets for every vertex's position (and optionally its normal); the mesh shows base + sum(weight * offset). Weights are usually 0 to 1 but can go beyond.

new MorphTargets(mesh, targets) makes a copy of the mesh that is yours to change: set weights, call update(), and draw morph.mesh instead of the original. Every character can have its own, since each makes its own copy of the vertices (the indices, texture coordinates and skin weights are shared). It works on skinned meshes too: the shape changes first and the skeleton then moves the result. Presentation only, like the rest of animation: it may use ordinary maths.

constructor(mesh, targets, { weights } = {})

The number of targets.

The number of a target from its name (or the number itself); throws for one that does not exist.

Set all the weights at once (ArrayLike<number>, in target order; missing ones become 0).

Move the weights toward a goal by at most rate per second (a smile that eases in); returns true while any weight is still on its way.

src/decal.js:56

function function createDynamicResolution({ target = 60, min = 0.4, step = 0.05, grace = 4 } = {})

Dynamic resolution: the share of the screen's size the 3D picture is drawn at, kept where the card can manage the frame rate. How long a frame takes follows the number of pixels, so the picture shrinks by about the square root of how far the frame rate is below the target, grows back slowly when the card keeps up, and waits longer before trying again after a try that failed. Frames of the first seconds (loading), of a hidden page and a single long stall do not count against the card. Give it the frame rate over the last half second every half second; draw the 3D picture at renderer.setRenderScale(drs.scale) and the writing and the controls at the screen's own size.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
o optional{target?: number, min?: number, step?: number, grace?: number}target frames a second to aim for (60), min the smallest share (0.4), step how much it grows by (0.05), grace seconds after starting (or coming back to the page) in which a slow frame rate is put down to loading (4).

Bundle levels of detail. levels run from the most detailed: each says the screen size (the height of the thing as a fraction of the height of the view, 0..1) *below which* it is replaced by the next one. The last level is used all the way down to cullBelow, under which nothing is drawn. Or give ratios and a mesh and the levels are made for you with simplifyMesh.

``js const tree = createLod({ mesh: highTree, ratios: [0.35, 0.12], screens: [0.25, 0.08], cullBelow: 0.01 }); // levels: highTree while taller than a quarter of the screen, 35% of its triangles from 25% down to 8%, 12% below that, nothing under 1% list.addLod(tree, model); ``

Copy the movement of a pose of one skeleton onto another. src/lighting.js:129

function function simplifyMesh(mesh, { ratio, cellSize, keepEdges = false, name } = {})

Make a coarser copy of a mesh by vertex clustering: the mesh is cut into a grid of cells, the vertices in a cell become one (their average), triangles that collapse to a line or a point are dropped. It is fast (linear in the size of the mesh), never fails on messy meshes, and works on skinned meshes (the joints of a cluster's vertices are blended and the four strongest kept). It rounds off small features and sharp corners as the cells grow, which is what a distant LOD should do.

Give ratio (0..1: the fraction of triangles to keep, found by trying cell sizes) or cellSize (metres, exactly). Texture seams may smear a little at coarse levels, and a mesh with hard edges (a box with a normal per face) is rounded off unless you pass keepEdges: true, which keeps vertices with very different normals apart (at the price of fewer triangles saved on smooth surfaces and tiny cracks between clusters).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
meshimport('./mesh.js').Mesh
o optional{ratio?: number, cellSize?: number, keepEdges?: boolean, name?: string}

Returns import('./mesh.js').Mesh

function function solveChain(skeleton, pose, chain, target, { iterations = 16, tolerance = 1e-4, weight = 1 } = {})

Reach a target with a chain of joints, each the child of the one before (FABRIK: the chain is pulled to the target from its tip and then pinned back to its root, a few times over). The root of the chain stays put and bone lengths are kept; a target out of reach stretches the chain straight toward it. Good for tails, spines, necks, tentacles, ropes and for arms or legs where you do not need a pole. Edits the rotations of every joint in the chain but the last.

function function solveTwoBone(skeleton, pose, { root, mid, end, target, pole, weight = 1, endRotation })

Reach a target with a three-joint limb (an arm: shoulder, elbow, wrist; a leg: hip, knee, ankle) by the exact two-bone solution: the limb bends at the middle joint, in the plane that holds the pole point, and stretches straight toward a target that is out of reach (it never overextends or folds past straight). Edits the rotations of root and mid in pose. mid must be a child of root and end a child of mid.

type GltfImage

glTF 2.0 and GLB loading: triangle meshes with positions, optional normals and indices, a base colour per material, the node hierarchy (transforms), and skeletal animation (skins with joint weights, and translation/rotation/scale clips for the joints). Right-handed, +y up, the same conventions as the engine. Materials: every material is read in full, the way glTF describes a surface: base colour, metallic and roughness, and the five kinds of picture (base colour, metallic-roughness, normal, occlusion, emissive), with the factors that multiply them, the alpha mode (opaque, cut-out or blended) and KHR_materials_emissive_strength. loadGltfTextures decodes the images into a TextureSet, loadGltfMaterials turns the materials into a MaterialSet, and addGltfToDrawList then draws with physically based lighting; without those two calls a model is drawn as before, with its base colour and base colour picture under the simple lighting. Texture coordinates (TEXCOORD_0) are read. Not supported (reported in warnings, or thrown when the file cannot be read at all): a second set of coordinates, texture transforms and samplers (images always repeat and are filtered), double-sided surfaces (drawn single-sided), sorting of blended surfaces, animations of plain nodes (only skin joints and morph weights animate), cameras and lights; cubic-spline animation is read as linear; Draco compression throws. Sparse accessors are read. Morph targets (blend shapes: positions and normals, with the starting weights and names) are read onto each instance's morph; createGltfMorph(instance) turns them into a MorphTargets you set weights on, and model.morphClips holds the file's weight animations. Compressed models are read: EXT_meshopt_compression (what gltfpack writes; see meshopt.js, no WebAssembly needed) and KHR_mesh_quantization (positions, normals and coordinates stored as 8 or 16-bit numbers, which is only a matter of reading them as they are, and of the node's scale putting positions back).

type GltfResult

glTF 2.0 and GLB loading: triangle meshes with positions, optional normals and indices, a base colour per material, the node hierarchy (transforms), and skeletal animation (skins with joint weights, and translation/rotation/scale clips for the joints). Right-handed, +y up, the same conventions as the engine. Materials: every material is read in full, the way glTF describes a surface: base colour, metallic and roughness, and the five kinds of picture (base colour, metallic-roughness, normal, occlusion, emissive), with the factors that multiply them, the alpha mode (opaque, cut-out or blended) and KHR_materials_emissive_strength. loadGltfTextures decodes the images into a TextureSet, loadGltfMaterials turns the materials into a MaterialSet, and addGltfToDrawList then draws with physically based lighting; without those two calls a model is drawn as before, with its base colour and base colour picture under the simple lighting. Texture coordinates (TEXCOORD_0) are read. Not supported (reported in warnings, or thrown when the file cannot be read at all): a second set of coordinates, texture transforms and samplers (images always repeat and are filtered), double-sided surfaces (drawn single-sided), sorting of blended surfaces, animations of plain nodes (only skin joints and morph weights animate), cameras and lights; cubic-spline animation is read as linear; Draco compression throws. Sparse accessors are read. Morph targets (blend shapes: positions and normals, with the starting weights and names) are read onto each instance's morph; createGltfMorph(instance) turns them into a MorphTargets you set weights on, and model.morphClips holds the file's weight animations. Compressed models are read: EXT_meshopt_compression (what gltfpack writes; see meshopt.js, no WebAssembly needed) and KHR_mesh_quantization (positions, normals and coordinates stored as 8 or 16-bit numbers, which is only a matter of reading them as they are, and of the node's scale putting positions back).

type PostOptions

NameTypeDescription
bloom optionalfalse | {threshold?: number, knee?: number, intensity?: number, levels?: number, radius?: number}Glow around bright areas. threshold is the brightness above which things glow (default 0.85), knee how softly it starts (0.5), intensity how much is added back (0.5), levels how many times the image is halved (5; more levels, wider glow), radius scales the blur (1).
exposure optionalnumberBrightness multiplier before tone mapping (1).
tonemap optional'none' | 'reinhard' | 'aces' | 'filmic'How values above 1 are squeezed into the displayable range ('aces').
contrast optionalnumber1 = unchanged; more pushes darks and lights apart, around mid grey.
saturation optionalnumber1 = unchanged, 0 = grey, above 1 = more vivid.
lift optionalnumber[][r, g, b] added to the dark end (0, 0, 0). gamma: mid-tone power per channel (1, 1, 1). gain: multiplier per channel (1, 1, 1): the colour grade.
gamma optionalnumber[]
gain optionalnumber[]
vignette optionalfalse | {strength?: number, radius?: number}Darkened corners; radius is where it starts, 0 (centre) to 1 (corner) (0.55).
dither optionalnumberNoise of this many 1/255 steps, hiding banding in smooth gradients (1; 0 turns it off).
ao optionalboolean | {radius?: number, intensity?: number, bias?: number, power?: number, samples?: number, scale?: number}Ambient occlusion (off unless given): creases, contact points and the undersides of things get darker, as they would with light bouncing around. radius is how far, in world units, it looks for things in the way (0.5), intensity 0..1 how dark it goes (1), power how sharply (1.5), bias the depth difference ignored so that flat surfaces do not shade themselves (0.03), samples the quality (12; 4 to 32), scale the size of the working image as a fraction of the screen (1; 0.5 is four times cheaper and a little softer). It darkens the lit picture (not only the ambient light), so keep it subtle on bright scenes.
ssr optionalboolean | {strength?: number, distance?: number, steps?: number, thickness?: number, minUp?: number, below?: number, above?: number, glass?: number, base?: number, glassBase?: number}Screen-space reflections (off unless given): surfaces that face up (a sea, a wet floor, a roof) show what is on the screen above them, found by marching a ray from each pixel through the depth buffer. strength 0..1 how much of the reflection is mixed in at the most (0.6; it is weaker where the surface is seen head on and strongest at a grazing angle, as a real one is), distance how far the ray goes, in world units (80), steps the quality (32; 8 to 64), thickness how far behind a surface the ray may go and still count as hitting it (1.5), minUp how level a surface must be to reflect, as the cosine of its angle from straight up (0.85), and below and above the heights (world y) between which things reflect (everywhere): a sea is below: 1. Only what is on the screen can be reflected, and a reflection that would leave it fades at the edges. There is no roughness here, so it suits smooth surfaces: limit it with below or above to the ones that are. glass (0: none) is the strength on the meshes the draw list marks with reflect(mesh) (glass towers, mirrors): they reflect on any facing and at any height. They are marked in the alpha channel of the scene, which the pass reads: a scene cleared to a transparent colour would count everything as marked, so clear to an opaque one. base (0.25) and glassBase (0.35) are how much of the reflection shows even head on, as a share of the strength; the rest comes with the angle (up to all of it at a grazing one).
dof optionalboolean | {focus?: number, range?: number, aperture?: number, maxBlur?: number, taps?: number}Depth of field (off unless given): things away from the focus distance (world units from the camera, 10) blur. range is the depth either side of the focus that stays sharp (0), aperture how fast the blur grows with the distance from the focus (1), maxBlur the largest blur radius in pixels (8), taps the quality (24; 8 to 64).
heat optional{x: number, y: number, radius: number, strength?: number}[]Heat haze (off unless given): the picture shimmers and wobbles round up to 16 hot places, such as an exhaust, a fire or a blast. x and y are where the place is on the screen, 0 to 1 from the left and from the top; radius how far the haze reaches, as a share of the screen's height; strength how far the picture is pushed at the middle, as a share of the screen's height (0.004, a few pixels, if left out). The haze fades smoothly to nothing at the edge of the radius. It is a distortion of the finished scene (nothing is hidden behind it, and a hot place behind a wall still shimmers: the caller decides which places to give).
heatTime optionalnumberThe clock of the shimmer, in seconds (0): give the time of the game so that the haze moves.
fxaa optionalbooleanFast approximate anti-aliasing of the finished picture (off). It smooths the edges that multisampling (the renderer's antialias) cannot, such as the edges inside textures and of tone-mapped highlights, and works with antialias: false. It softens fine detail slightly.

type ShadowOptions

Directional-light shadow mapping, shared by the WebGPU and WebGL2 renderers. One orthographic depth map of the world seen from the light, fitted to a box around the camera's view: everything that can cast a shadow is drawn into it from the light's point of view, and the main pass asks, for each pixel, whether something is between it and the light (a 3x3 percentage-closer filter softens the edge).

NameTypeDescription
size optionalnumberShadow map resolution in texels per side (default 2048).
radius optionalnumberHalf the width of the covered box in metres, centred ahead of the camera (default 45). A bigger radius covers more of the world with coarser shadows: texel size is 2 * radius / size.
bias optionalnumberDepth bias in light-space depth units (default 0.0004: about 8 cm over the default 200 m depth range).
strength optionalnumber0..1, how dark shadows are (default 0.75; the rest is ambient light that shadows never remove).
cascades optionalnumberSplit the covered area into this many nested boxes (1 to 4, default 1), each with its own shadow map of size: the nearest is small and very sharp, the farthest is radius. Shadows near the camera get far more detail for the same cost per pixel.
ratio optionalnumberEach cascade is this fraction of the size of the next one out (0.15 to 0.9, default 0.35).

@engine/replay 0.1.0

Replays and spectating: record a match as compact snapshot deltas (seek anywhere, any speed) or as its inputs (a few KB, with drift detection), a delayed feed shared by any number of spectators.

10 of 10 exports have a description. npm install @engine/replay

class class InputPlayer

Plays an input recording back through your simulation: it hands your step the recorded inputs, tick by tick, checking the recorded hashes as it goes. It can jump to any tick (it restores the nearest saved state before it with load and plays forward from there), run faster or slower, pause and loop.

constructor(replay, { step, load = null, hash = null, onDesync = null })
NameTypeDescription
replayobject | stringWhat InputRecorder.finish() returned, or its text.
oobject
o.step(inputs: any, tick: number) => voidRun one tick of the game with these inputs.
o.load optional(state: any) => voidPut the game into a saved state (needed to seek, to start from a state other than the game's fresh one, and to loop).
o.hash optional() => anyThe same function the recording used, to check the replay still matches (without it nothing is verified).
o.onDesync optional(error: ReplayDesyncError) => voidCalled when a hash differs. Without it the error is thrown from advance / update.
get endTick
get finished
inputsAt(tick)

The recorded inputs of a tick.

rewind()

Put the game at the start of the recording: the first checkpoint, if there is one (otherwise the game must be fresh).

advance(n = 1)

Run n ticks (stops at the end). Returns how many ran.

seek(tick)

Jump so that the next tick to run is tick (clamped): restores the nearest saved state at or before it, then plays forward. Needs load and a recorded save.

update(dt)

Play along for dt real seconds (times speed, unless paused). Returns how many ticks ran.

src/inputs.js:79

class class InputRecorder

Records a match of a deterministic game as its inputs: the starting state, then what each player pressed on each tick. Because the simulation gives the same result every time (that is what the fixed timestep and @engine/math are for), playing the inputs back through it reproduces the whole match, and a ten-minute match is a few kilobytes. Every checkpointEvery ticks it also keeps a copy of the game state (so a player can jump into the middle) and every hashEvery ticks a hash of it (so a replay that has stopped matching, after an update changed the rules, is caught at once, not by someone noticing the wrong ending). Call record(tick, inputs) at the start of every tick, before the simulation runs it, with whatever your simulation takes as input for that tick (anything JSON-able: a map from player to buttons). Ticks must be consecutive.

constructor({ game = '', version = 1, tickRate = 60, meta = {}, save = null, hash = null, checkpointEvery = 600, hashEvery = 60 })
NameTypeDescription
oobject
o.game optionalstringName of the game, stored.
o.version optionalnumberVersion of the game's rules (1): a replay of another version is refused by the player's caller, not guessed at.
o.tickRate optionalnumberTicks per second (60).
o.meta optionalRecord<string, any>Anything about the match (map, players, seed, date).
o.save optional() => anyReturns the game state as plain data (it is copied by JSON), for checkpoints. Without it the replay can only be played from the start.
o.hash optional() => anyReturns a number or string that is the same whenever the game state is the same, for catching drift. Default: hashState(save()) if save is given.
o.checkpointEvery optionalnumberTicks between saved states (600).
o.hashEvery optionalnumberTicks between hashes (60).

The number of ticks recorded.

class class ReplayPlayer

Plays a replay back. Give it the bytes (a file, or what ReplayRecorder.finish() returned) and the schema it was recorded with; call update(dt) each frame, and draw history (the same SnapshotHistory a live client draws from, so interpolation code is shared: history.around(player.tickAt)). Seek anywhere, change speed, pause, loop. A recording cut short by a crash plays up to where it stopped (truncated is true).

class class ReplayRecorder

Records a match as a stream of snapshots, in the same compact delta form the network uses, so five minutes of a world of forty entities is about 1 to 3 megabytes (a full snapshot every keyframeEvery ticks makes it possible to jump to any moment without playing everything before it). Game events (a kill, a chat line, a round start) can be recorded between the frames. It records what the server sent to a viewer (or the full world), so it plays back on any machine, even one whose simulation would not reproduce the match; for a deterministic game that wants tiny files, see InputRecorder.

class class SpectatorFeed

Watching a match: the server keeps the whole world for spectators, a few seconds behind what the players are doing (so nobody can tell a team where the enemy is), and sends it to any number of viewers. All spectators who have the same snapshot as a starting point get the same bytes, so the cost of a hundred spectators is a few encodes, not a hundred. Each tick, push the full-world snapshot. Each time you send to a spectator, ask for packet(spectatorId, ackTick) (the newest tick that spectator says it has) and send the bytes as they are. The packets have the same layout as a player's snapshot packets (MSG.SNAPSHOT, input ack 0, the delta), so a spectator's client can read them with the normal client code or SnapshotReceiver.

class class CloudSync

Cloud saves: sync() brings the slots on the device and on the server into step, in both directions, without ever losing a save. Both sides are {get, set, delete, keys} storages, so the server can be HttpStorage (with createSaveHandler on your own server, or anything that speaks the same few requests), a folder, or another device's storage in a test. For each slot, it compares the two files with a record, kept on the device, of the file both sides held when they last agreed: only the device changed: upload; only the server changed: download; the same on both: nothing; both changed (played offline on two devices): a conflict, settled by strategy. Before a file is replaced on either side the old one is kept as .bak, as SaveGame does, so even a wrong choice can be undone by hand.

constructor({ local, remote, strategy = 'newest', prefix = 'slot.', ledgerPrefix = 'sync.', deletions = false })
NameTypeDescription
oobject
o.local{get: Function, set: Function, delete: Function, keys: Function}The device's storage (the one the SaveGame uses).
o.remote{get: Function, set: Function, delete: Function, keys: Function}The server's.
o.strategy optional'newest' | 'local' | 'remote' | 'ask' | ((local: any, remote: any, info: {slot: string}) => 'local' | 'remote' | any | Promise<any>)What to do when both sides changed: 'newest' (the default) keeps the save with the later savedAt (ties go to the one with more play time), 'local' / 'remote' always keep that side, 'ask' writes nothing and reports the conflict for the player to settle (resolve(slot, 'local' | 'remote')), or a function that gets both decoded save files and returns 'local', 'remote', or a merged save file object (written to both sides).
o.prefix optionalstringOnly slots whose key starts with this (default slot.: every SaveGame slot).
o.ledgerPrefix optionalstringWhere the record of the last agreement is kept on the device (sync.).
o.deletions optionalbooleanWhether a slot deleted on one side is deleted on the other (false: a missing slot is brought back from the side that has it).

type SlotInfo

What CloudSync did, or found, for one slot. - same: both sides hold the same save. uploaded / downloaded: the older side (or the side without the slot) was brought up to date. deleted: the slot was deleted on one side and, with deletions, now on the other (from says where it was deleted). - conflict: both sides changed since they last agreed and nothing was written (with strategy: 'ask', or a merge that declined): local and remote describe both. - resolved: it was a conflict, and the strategy chose (chose says which side, or merged). - failed: a side could not be reached or a file was unreadable (error).

type SyncResult

What CloudSync did, or found, for one slot. - same: both sides hold the same save. uploaded / downloaded: the older side (or the side without the slot) was brought up to date. deleted: the slot was deleted on one side and, with deletions, now on the other (from says where it was deleted). - conflict: both sides changed since they last agreed and nothing was written (with strategy: 'ask', or a merge that declined): local and remote describe both. - resolved: it was a conflict, and the strategy chose (chose says which side, or merged). - failed: a side could not be reached or a file was unreadable (error).

class class ClientReplicator

Everything the server remembers and decides for ONE client's replication.

A client's "view" is the snapshot it was sent: only the entities it is interested in, and (when a bandwidth budget is set) not all of them freshly updated, because far-away, low-priority entities may carry slightly older values. So deltas are computed against the *views we actually sent* (kept in a per-client history, keyed by tick), not against the world.

Per tick: setVisible (who), buildView (what values, within budget), encode (bytes + history).

Budget: each unsent entity accumulates priority (faster when near), the highest-priority ones get fresh values, and an AIMD controller adjusts how many per tick so the measured bytes/second tracks the budget. The client's own entity and entities it has never seen are always fresh.

class class ProcessRoom extends ChannelRoom

A room in its own OS process, connected to the gateway by an IPC channel.

Containment beyond a worker thread: a heap cap (memoryMb) so a leaking or hostile room dies alone (V8 aborts the process, the gateway sees the exit and reports it), a scrubbed environment, optional Node permission-model confinement (confine), and lower scheduling priority if asked. Creates, finds and retires rooms, and routes incoming connections to them. - Rooms are created on demand (autoCreate) up to maxRooms, each with at most maxPlayers. - A connection that arrives while its room is still starting is held (its early packets are buffered and replayed) until the room is ready. - Empty rooms are closed after idleCloseMs. - A room that crashes disconnects only its own players; the next join to that name starts a fresh room.

src/room-host.js:127

Types

type RoomHandle

The gateway-side handle on one room. Three implementations share this interface so a game can choose isolation per deployment without changing room code:

- ProcessRoom: the room runs in its own OS process. Strongest containment: a crash, a runaway allocation (per-room heap cap), a native fault or a hang kills only that process, and the OS can limit it further. - WorkerRoom: the room runs in its own worker thread. Nothing is shared; a slow or crashing room cannot stall or take down the gateway or other rooms, but a native crash or out-of-memory still takes the whole process. - InlineRoom: the room runs in this thread (cheapest, no message passing; one room can stall the others).

A room module exports createRoom(options) returning { attach(transport), close?(), stats?(), control?(data) }.

NameTypeDescription
namestring
mode'process' | 'worker' | 'inline'
readyPromise<void>Resolves when the room can accept players.
playersnumberConnected players.
join(conn: import('../../transport/src/index.js').Transport) => void
control(data: any) => voidSend a control message to the room module (room.control).
stats() => anyLatest statistics reported by the room.
stop() => Promise<void>
onExit((reason: string) => void) | nullCalled once if the room ends without stop() (crash).

src/rtc/signaling.js:96

constant const CHANNEL

Transport contract. Every adapter (in-memory, WebSocket, WebTransport...) implements Transport for one connection and Listener for a server.

Channels: - RELIABLE: ordered and lossless (handshake, spawn/despawn, chat). - UNRELIABLE: may be dropped, duplicated or reordered (snapshots, inputs). Payloads must carry their own tick/sequence so stale or duplicate messages can be discarded. A WebSocket adapter maps both channels onto one ordered stream, so a lost packet delays later ones; newer snapshots supersede older ones, so receivers should just drop anything stale.

send copies the bytes (or finishes with them) before returning, so callers may reuse their buffer immediately.

Value: Object.freeze({ RELIABLE: 0, UNRELIABLE: 1 })

node class class FrameParser

Incremental frame parser and message assembler. Feed it socket chunks with push; it calls back with complete binary messages and control frames, and throws WsError on any violation (the caller closes with err.code). Text frames are rejected (1003): this transport is binary only. Extensions (RSV bits) are never negotiated, so any RSV bit is a violation.

src/ui.js:24

class class Widget

A node in the UI tree. Containers lay their children out (see layout.js); leaf widgets (label, button, ...) measure and draw themselves. Everything is in logical pixels; the Ui applies the scale.

Style (all optional): - direction: 'column' (default), 'row' or 'stack' (children overlap, placed by anchor). - gap, padding (number, [vertical, horizontal] or [top, right, bottom, left]). - align: cross axis, 'stretch' (default), 'start', 'center', 'end'. justify: main axis, 'start' (default), 'center', 'end', 'between'. - width / height: a number, or 'fill' (take the free space); grow: share of free space along the parent's main axis; minWidth, minHeight, maxWidth, maxHeight; alignSelf overrides the parent's align for this child. - anchor (children of a 'stack'): 'fill' (default), 'center', 'top', 'bottom', 'left', 'right', 'top-left', 'top-right', 'bottom-left', 'bottom-right'; offsetX, offsetY. - background, border: packed colours (or true for the theme's panel colours); radius.

src/layout.js:42

function function attachAccessibility(ui, { document: doc = globalThis.document, host = null, label = 'Game menu', field = null } = {})

Mirror the UI in the page for assistive technology. The canvas is invisible to a screen reader; this builds a hidden, always up to date set of real elements with the right ARIA roles (buttons, switches, sliders, text fields, lists, headings, dialogs) that it can read and operate: activating one clicks the widget, the arrow keys on a slider go through the same key handling as for everyone else, and moving the screen reader's cursor onto a control moves the UI's focus there. Announcements (ui.announce) go to live regions; opening a screen announces its name. Also sets ui.reducedMotion from the system's reduced-motion setting. Call the returned update() once a frame (it only touches what changed).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
uiimport('./ui.js').Ui
o optionalobject
o.document optionalDocument
o.host optionalHTMLElementWhere the mirror is put (default the end of the body).
o.label optionalstringWhat the whole region is called ("Game menu").
o.field optional() => HTMLElement | nullThe page's hidden text field, if you use attachDom (() => dom.input), so it can be labelled with the widget it is editing.

Returns {update: () => void, detach: () => void, element: HTMLElement}

type A11yNode

What a screen reader is told about one widget.

NameTypeDescription
idstringStable for the widget while it lives (its id style, or one made for it).
role'button' | 'switch' | 'slider' | 'spinbutton' | 'textbox' | 'listbox' | 'option' | 'progressbar' | 'text' | 'heading' | 'separator' | 'group' | 'dialog'
namestringWhat it is called ("Music volume", "Resume").
description optionalstringExtra help ("Type a room name").
value optionalstringWhat it holds, as it should be read ("50%", "Hard"); never the text of a password.
valueNow optionalnumber
valueMin optionalnumber
valueMax optionalnumberFor sliders, spin buttons and progress bars.
checked optionalbooleanFor switches.
selected optionalbooleanFor options.
level optionalnumberFor headings (1 is the biggest).
password optionalboolean
disabledboolean
focusedboolean
focusableboolean
modalbooleanFor dialogs.
bounds{x: number, y: number, w: number, h: number}Where it is on screen, in CSS pixels (for a screen magnifier or a touch explorer).
childrenA11yNode[]
widgetWidgetThe widget itself (so a front end can act on it).

type A11yOptions

Optional help for the screen reader, set on any widget: widget.a11y = { label, description, role, hidden, live }. label replaces the name worked out from its text, description adds help, role overrides the role, hidden: true leaves a decorative widget out, and live: 'polite' | 'assertive' makes changes to a text widget be announced.

type Painter

What the UI draws with (see painter.js for ready-made ones). Sizes and positions are in screen pixels.

Everything a widget needs to look like part of one game: colours (packed, see color.js), text sizes and spacing, in logical pixels. Pass overrides to createTheme; anything left out keeps the default, so a game restyles only what it cares about.
